Apple___Apple_scab.cause: Caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. It thrives in cool, wet spring weather when temperatures are between 10–24°C and moisture persists on leaves for 9+ hours.
Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves and fruit. Infected leaves may curl and fall prematurely.

treatments.ratio: Neem Oil : Water = 1:50 ratio (20ml per litre)

prevention: Choose disease-resistant varieties when planting new crops — ask your local nursery for scab-resistant options
Prune branches every season to allow good airflow between leaves, which helps them dry quickly after rain
Collect and burn all fallen leaves in autumn — the fungus survives winter in dead leaves on the ground
Water your plants at the base, not from above — wet leaves help the fungus spread faster
Spray a preventive fungicide (like Bordeaux mixture) before the rainy season starts

Apple___Black_rot.cause: Caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. Infects through wounds and enters bark during warm, humid weather (24–29°C).
Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Brown circular lesions on leaves with purple margins. Fruit shows 'frog-eye' leaf spots and eventually turns black.
prevention: Cut and remove infected branches — cut at least 15cm (6 inches) below where you can see the disease
Remove all shrivelled or mummified fruit from the tree and the ground — these carry the fungus
Always clean your cutting tools with bleach solution (1 part bleach, 9 parts water) before and after pruning
Avoid injuring the bark of trees — wounds are the main entry point for this fungus
Apply a protective fungicide spray right after pruning to protect fresh cuts from infection

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause: Caused by the fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. Requires two hosts — cedar/juniper and apple trees — to complete its life cycle.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces with tube-like spore structures underneath.
prevention: If you have cedar or juniper trees growing nearby, try to remove them — this disease needs both types of trees to survive
Choose rust-resistant crop varieties when planting new trees — your local agriculture office can suggest good options
Start spraying fungicide early in spring when buds first appear, before you see any orange spots
Check your plants regularly during the rainy season and remove any infected leaves immediately
Keep good spacing between your plants so air can flow freely and leaves dry quickly

Apple___healthy.symptoms: Leaves appear green, vibrant, and free of spots or discolouration.
prevention: Keep feeding your plants with a balanced fertilizer (NPK) according to the season
Prune your plants regularly to keep good airflow and sunlight reaching all leaves
Check your plants every week, especially during monsoon season, for any early signs of spots or discolouration
Water at the base of plants early in the morning so leaves stay dry during the day
Remove any weeds growing around your plants as they can harbour pests and diseases

Background_without_leaves.cause: The uploaded image does not appear to contain a clear leaf. Please upload a photo of a single plant leaf for accurate disease detection.
prevention: Take a close-up photo of a single leaf against a plain background
Make sure the leaf fills most of the photo frame
Use good lighting — natural daylight works best
Avoid blurry photos — hold your phone steady when taking the picture

Blueberry___healthy.symptoms: Plant looks healthy with vibrant foliage.
prevention: Keep soil slightly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) by adding compost or natural acidifiers
Spread mulch (like pine bark or straw) around the base of plants to keep soil moist and cool
Water regularly but do not let the soil become waterlogged — good drainage is very important
Check your plants weekly for any early signs of leaf spots or wilting
Remove dead or weak branches to allow sunlight and fresh air to reach all parts of the plant

Cherry___Powdery_mildew.cause: Caused by the fungus Podosphaera clandestina. Favours dry conditions with high humidity, temperatures between 15–27°C, and poor air circulation.
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery coating on young leaves, shoots, and fruit. Leaves may curl and distort.

treatments.ratio: 1 tablespoon per litre of water + few drops dish soap

prevention: Prune your plants regularly so that air can move freely between branches — this stops the fungus from growing
Do not use too much nitrogen fertilizer, as it creates soft new leaves that are easily attacked by this disease
Choose disease-resistant varieties when planting — ask at your local seed shop
Water your plants at the base in the early morning, never from the top
Remove and destroy any leaves showing white powdery coating immediately — do not throw them near your field

Cherry___healthy.symptoms: Healthy, vibrant foliage with no visible lesions.
prevention: Continue regular pruning to maintain plant shape and airflow
Apply balanced fertilizer based on the crop's growth stage
Check for any pest activity like caterpillars or aphids every few days
Keep the area around your plants clean and weed-free
Water early in the morning so leaves can dry out during the day

Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.cause: Caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. Favoured by warm (25–30°C), humid, cloudy weather with extended periods of leaf wetness.
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.symptoms: Tan to gray rectangular lesions parallel to leaf veins. Severe infections can cause significant yield loss.
prevention: Plant disease-resistant varieties or hybrids — ask your seed dealer for gray leaf spot resistant options
Practice crop rotation — do not grow the same crop in the same field year after year, alternate with different crops
After harvest, plough the field deeply to bury old plant waste — the fungus lives in leftover crop debris
Keep proper spacing between plants so air flows well and leaves dry faster after rain or dew
Scout your field regularly during humid weather and act quickly if you see any tan or gray spots on leaves

Corn___Common_rust.cause: Caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. Spreads via airborne spores in cool (16–23°C), humid conditions with heavy dew.
Corn___Common_rust.symptoms: Small, circular to elongated, brick-red pustules on both leaf surfaces.
prevention: Choose rust-tolerant varieties when buying seeds — these are widely available and your seed shop can help you select
Walk through your field regularly during cool, wet weather and look for small reddish-brown bumps on leaves
Spray fungicide at the very first sign of rust — early treatment gives the best results
Remove and burn heavily infected plants to stop the disease from spreading to healthy ones
Avoid planting too close together — good spacing helps leaves dry quickly and slows the spread of fungus spores

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cause: Caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. Favoured by moderate temperatures (18–27°C) and extended periods of humid weather.
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Long (2.5–15 cm), elliptical, tan-gray lesions on leaves. Can cause 30–50% yield loss in severe cases.

treatments.ratio: 1ml each per litre of water (tank mix)

prevention: Choose resistant varieties or hybrids — this is the most effective and cheapest way to control this disease
Rotate your crops — grow a different crop (like pulses or vegetables) in the same field next season
After harvest, plough deeply to bury the old plant stalks and leaves where the fungus hides
If you see long, oval-shaped gray spots on lower leaves, act fast — spray fungicide before it spreads to upper leaves
Maintain good field drainage so that water does not collect around plants

Corn___healthy.symptoms: Tall, vibrant plants with dark green leaves.
prevention: Continue feeding your crop with proper nitrogen fertilizer at the right growth stages
Walk through your field every week and check for any pest damage or unusual spots on leaves
Keep adequate spacing between plants — overcrowding leads to poor airflow and more diseases
Water your plants at the base, avoiding splashing water on leaves
After harvest, remove all plant waste from the field to prevent diseases from carrying over to the next season

Grape___Black_rot.cause: Caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. Thrives in warm (21–26°C), rainy weather. Spores are released during rainfall.
Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Reddish-brown circular lesions on leaves with dark borders. Fruit shrivels into hard, black 'mummies'.
prevention: Collect and destroy all shrivelled (mummified) fruit — they carry the fungus and will reinfect your crop next season
Prune your plants to open up the canopy so sunlight and air can reach the inner parts, which helps leaves dry faster
Start spraying protective fungicides early in the season, even before you see any symptoms — prevention is key
Remove all infected leaves and fruit from the ground around your plants
Train and tie your vines properly so they are not too dense and have good air circulation

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cause: Caused by a complex of wood-rotting fungi (Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp.). Enters through pruning wounds in cool, moist conditions.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).symptoms: Interveinal leaf chlorosis with reddish-brown margins (tiger stripe). Fruit shows dark spotting. Vine may suddenly wilt and die (apoplexy).

treatments.ratio: Apply paste on fresh pruning wounds

prevention: Always seal pruning cuts immediately with Bordeaux paste or wound sealant — the fungus enters through open wounds
Only prune during dry weather — never prune when it is raining or the bark is wet
If a vine is severely infected, remove it completely and burn it — do not leave infected wood in your field
Delay pruning to late in the season to reduce the chance of fungal spore entry
Clean your pruning tools with bleach solution (1 part bleach, 9 parts water) before cutting each vine

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.cause: Caused by the fungus Isariopsis clavispora (Pseudocercospora vitis). Spreads in warm, humid, rainy conditions.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on leaves. Severe infections cause leaf drop, weakening the vine.
prevention: Keep your plants properly pruned and trained so that air flows freely through the leaves — this helps them dry after rain
Do not use overhead sprinklers — water only at the base of plants to keep leaves dry
Start spraying fungicides before the monsoon season begins, as a preventive measure
Remove and destroy all fallen leaves and plant waste from the field to reduce fungal spores
Avoid overcrowding your plants — leave enough space between them for good sunlight and airflow

Grape___healthy.symptoms: Vibrant green leaves, no spots or discolouration.
prevention: Keep your canopy well-managed by regular pruning and training of vines
Watch out for powdery mildew and downy mildew, especially during humid weather
Feed your plants with balanced nutrition — too much nitrogen can make leaves soft and prone to diseases
Check the underside of leaves regularly for any early signs of fungal growth
Maintain clean ground under your vines by removing fallen leaves and fruit debris

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: Caused by the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid insect. There is NO cure — infected trees must be removed.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Asymmetric yellowing (blotchy mottle) of leaves. Fruit is small, lopsided, bitter, and may have aborted seeds.

treatments.ratio: N/A — destroy and remove the infected plant immediately
0.5ml per litre of water, soil drench

prevention: This is a very serious disease with NO CURE — if your plant is infected, you must remove and burn it immediately to protect your other plants
Always buy plants only from certified, disease-free nurseries — never from unknown sources
Control the psyllid insect (a tiny flying pest) aggressively with regular insecticide sprays — this insect spreads the disease
Inspect all new plants carefully before planting them in your field — look for uneven yellowing on leaves
Keep your field and surrounding areas clean — remove any wild or abandoned plants that could harbour the disease

Peach___Bacterial_spot.cause: Caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. Spreads during warm (24–28°C), wet, windy weather.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown. Fruit shows cracked, sunken lesions.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties when planting — this is the most effective long-term solution
Water your plants at the base only, never from above — water splash spreads the bacteria very quickly
Prune your plants properly to allow good airflow — bacteria thrive in stagnant, moist conditions
Reduce any damage to plants from wind, hail, or insects — bacteria enter through wounds and injuries
Remove and destroy any infected leaves or fruit immediately — do not let them fall on the ground near healthy plants

Peach___healthy.symptoms: Healthy green leaves with no visible lesions.
prevention: Continue regular pruning to keep good airflow through the plant
Apply balanced fertilizer at the right time of year
Watch for bacterial spot symptoms after heavy rains — small dark spots on leaves
Keep your field clean and weed-free around the plants
Water in the early morning at the base of the plant

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.cause: Caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. Thrives in warm (24–30°C), wet, stormy conditions. Spreads rapidly by rain splash.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit that turn brown and scabby. Defoliation can occur.
prevention: Always use certified disease-free seeds or seedlings — buying cheap, uncertified seeds is the biggest risk
Practice crop rotation — do not grow the same type of crop in the same spot for 2 years in a row
Water only at the base of your plants, never from above — rain splash and water droplets are the main way this bacteria spreads
Stake or support your plants so they stand upright with good airflow around the leaves
Remove and burn any infected plants immediately — do not compost them, as the bacteria will survive

Pepper,_bell___healthy.symptoms: Vibrant, dark green leaves with no blemishes.
prevention: Maintain a consistent watering schedule — these plants do best with steady, even moisture
Use calcium-rich fertilizer to prevent blossom end rot, which causes the bottom of fruit to turn dark and mushy
Check regularly for aphids (small green or black insects) and whiteflies under the leaves
Keep your plants staked and off the ground for better air circulation
Add mulch around the base of plants to keep soil moisture steady and prevent weeds

Potato___Early_blight.cause: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Favours warm (24–29°C), dry days followed by wet nights with heavy dew. Commonly infects stressed or aging plants.
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown, circular spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older lower leaves. Causes premature defoliation.
prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves as soon as you see dark brown spots with ring patterns — do not wait
Water at the base of plants only, never wet the leaves — the fungus grows faster on wet leaf surfaces
Feed your plants well with balanced fertilizer — weak or stressed plants are attacked first
Rotate your crops — do not grow the same type of crop in the same spot year after year
Apply a protective fungicide spray before the disease season starts, especially if you had this disease last year

Potato___Late_blight.cause: Caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans — the pathogen behind the Irish Potato Famine. Spreads explosively in cool (10–20°C), wet, humid conditions.
Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked, pale green lesions on leaves that rapidly turn dark brown to black. White mold visible on leaf undersides in humid conditions.
prevention: WARNING: This is a VERY dangerous disease — it can destroy your entire crop in just a few days if not treated quickly
Use only certified disease-free seed tubers from trusted sources — infected seeds are the main starting point
Hill soil around the base of plants to protect tubers from getting infected through the soil
Never use overhead irrigation — wet leaves are the perfect environment for this disease to spread rapidly
Destroy all infected plants immediately — pull them out, bag them, and burn them. Do NOT compost them
Watch the weather closely — if you see cool, rainy, foggy conditions coming, spray your crop with a protective fungicide immediately

Potato___healthy.symptoms: Lush green foliage with no spots or wilting.
prevention: Continue hilling soil around the base of your plants as they grow — this protects the tubers
Feed with balanced NPK fertilizer at the right growth stages
Check your field every week for Colorado potato beetle and other pests
Maintain good drainage in your field so water does not pool around plants
Keep your field clean — remove weeds that can harbour pests and diseases

Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: Healthy canes with vibrant green leaves.
prevention: Prune old canes annually and allow new growth to take over — this keeps the plant healthy
Spread mulch around the base to keep soil moist and suppress weeds
In hot weather, check the underside of leaves for spider mites — they love dry, hot conditions
Water regularly at the base, especially during dry spells
Remove any dead or damaged canes promptly to prevent disease from starting

Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Lush, trifoliate leaves with healthy coloration.
prevention: Rotate crops with non-legume crops (like cereals) to break pest and disease cycles
Avoid planting in compacted soil — use deep tillage to improve root growth and drainage
Check regularly for soybean aphids and other pests, especially during warm weather
Ensure proper plant spacing for good airflow between plants
Keep your field borders clean and weed-free

Squash___Powdery_mildew.cause: Caused by the fungus Erysiphe cichoracearum and Sphaerotheca fuliginea. Thrives in warm (20–27°C), dry conditions with low soil moisture but high humidity.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White, powdery spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces. Leaves turn yellow and die as disease progresses.

treatments.ratio: 1 tbsp per litre of water + 0.5ml dish soap
3g wettable sulfur per litre of water
1 tsp baking soda + 1 tsp soap per litre

prevention: Choose disease-resistant varieties when buying seeds — many improved varieties are available that resist powdery mildew
Water only at the base of plants, never from above — but make sure the soil gets enough water to keep roots happy
Space your plants well apart so air can circulate freely between them — crowded plants are attacked first
Remove badly infected leaves immediately and burn them — do not leave them on the ground
You can make a simple home spray: mix 1 teaspoon baking soda + 1 teaspoon liquid soap in 1 litre of water and spray on leaves every few days as prevention

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.cause: Caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. Favours wet, cool conditions in spring and autumn.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Small, purple or reddish spots on leaves that expand into irregular scorched areas. Severe infections cause defoliation.
prevention: Remove old, dried-up foliage after harvest — this is where the fungus hides and waits for the next season
Water only at the base of plants — avoid getting water on the leaves as much as possible
Plant in well-drained locations — waterlogging around the roots weakens the plant and invites disease
Apply straw mulch around your plants — it prevents soil and fungal spores from splashing onto leaves during rain
Keep good spacing between plants so air can dry the leaves quickly after rain or dew
Replace your planting beds every 3–4 years with fresh soil and new plants for best yields
Keep straw mulch around plants to protect fruit and reduce disease splash from soil
In hot weather, check the underside of leaves for two-spotted spider mites (tiny red/brown dots)
Water regularly at the base of plants, especially during fruiting
Remove any runners you do not need to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cause: Caused by Xanthomonas species. Spreads rapidly during warm (24–30°C), rainy, stormy weather via rain splash.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves, stems, and fruit that turn dark brown with yellow halos.
prevention: Always use certified disease-free seeds from a trusted source — the bacteria can live on seeds for years
Water only at the base of plants — never use overhead sprinklers, as rain splash is the main way this disease spreads
Rotate your crops — do not plant the same type of crop in the same field two seasons in a row
Remove and burn all infected plant parts immediately — do not leave them in the field or compost them
After the season ends, clean your field thoroughly — remove all plant debris to eliminate hiding spots for bacteria

Tomato___Early_blight.cause: Caused by Alternaria solani. Attacks stressed, mature, or aging plants in warm (24–29°C), humid conditions.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings and yellow halos on lower, older leaves. Lesions spread upward.
prevention: Remove the lower infected leaves as soon as you spot dark brown spots with ring patterns — this stops it from climbing up the plant
Avoid wetting the leaves when watering — always water at the base of the plant
Spread mulch (straw or dry leaves) on the ground around your plants to prevent soil from splashing onto lower leaves
Keep your plants well-fed with balanced fertilizer — starving plants are attacked first
Rotate your crops — do not grow the same crop in the same spot year after year

Tomato___Late_blight.cause: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. Spreads catastrophically in cool (10–20°C), wet, foggy conditions. Highly infectious — can destroy an entire crop in days.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked dark lesions on leaves/stems. White mold on undersides. Fruit develops dark, greasy spots.
prevention: URGENT: This disease can wipe out your entire crop within days — treat it immediately if detected
Destroy all infected plants right away — pull them out completely, bag them, and burn them. Do NOT compost
Never wet the leaves when watering — use drip irrigation or water at the base only
Before blight-risk weather (cool, rainy, foggy), spray your healthy plants with a protective fungicide
Plant resistant varieties — ask your local agriculture centre for late blight resistant options
Do not plant next to fields that had this disease last season — the spores can travel through the air

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause: Caused by Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum). Common in greenhouse conditions with high humidity (>85%) and poor air circulation.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on upper leaf surface with olive-green to brown velvety mold on underside.
prevention: If growing in a greenhouse or polyhouse, reduce humidity below 85% by opening vents and doors during the day
Ensure good ventilation — use fans if needed to keep air moving around your plants
Remove and destroy any infected leaves immediately — look for olive-green velvety patches on the underside of leaves
Water only at the base of plants — wet leaves in a humid environment are perfect for this mold to grow
Space your plants properly and prune extra branches to improve air circulation

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. Most common after first fruit sets. Favours warm (20–25°C), wet, humid conditions.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Many small circular spots with dark borders and white/gray centers on lower leaves. Spreads rapidly upward.
prevention: Remove the lower infected leaves immediately — this disease starts at the bottom and moves up, so early removal saves the plant
Spread mulch on the ground around your plants to prevent fungal spores in the soil from splashing onto lower leaves
Stake or cage your plants to keep them upright and off the ground — this improves airflow and reduces infection risk
Rotate your crops every year — the fungus survives in old plant debris in the soil
Water at the base of the plant only, early in the morning so any moisture on leaves dries quickly

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Caused by Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae). These tiny pests thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions and multiply very rapidly.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Tiny yellow or white speckles on leaves. Fine webbing visible on the underside of leaves. Leaves turn bronze/brown and fall off.

treatments.ratio: 5ml liquid soap per litre of water
treatments.frequency: Every 3–5 days, spray on leaf underside
Once, repeat after 7 days if needed

prevention: Check the underside of leaves regularly — spider mites are very tiny but you can see their fine webs and yellow dots
Keep your plants well-watered — water-stressed plants are attacked first by spider mites
Spray water on the underside of leaves to wash off the mites — they hate moisture
Avoid using broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial predator insects which naturally eat spider mites
Keep your field clean and dust-free — dusty conditions favour spider mite outbreaks

Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. Thrives in warm, humid tropical and subtropical climates.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Circular lesions with concentric rings (target appearance) on leaves. Brown spots also appear on fruit and stems.
prevention: Remove infected leaves and any plant debris from the field — the fungus survives in old crop waste
If growing in a greenhouse, avoid high humidity by improving ventilation and air movement
Keep adequate spacing between your plants so air can move freely and leaves dry faster after rain
Rotate your crops — do not plant the same type of crop in the same field every season
Start applying protective fungicide early in the season, especially in warm and humid weather

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: A viral disease (TYLCV) transmitted by silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). No chemical cure exists. Early detection and vector control are critical.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of young leaves. Stunted plant growth. Flowers and fruit do not develop properly.

treatments.ratio: N/A — remove and destroy infected plants to prevent spread

prevention: This disease has NO CURE — once a plant is infected, it cannot be saved. Remove and burn infected plants immediately
Control whiteflies aggressively — they are the tiny white flying insects that spread this virus from plant to plant
Use yellow sticky traps in your field to catch whiteflies early (available at most agricultural supply shops)
Use insect-proof nets to cover your seedling nursery — this prevents whiteflies from infecting young plants
Plant resistant varieties — ask your local seed dealer for virus-resistant options
Do not plant near fields that already have this disease — the virus can spread quickly through whiteflies

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Caused by Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV), highly stable and spread by contact (hands, tools, insects). No chemical cure.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves. Leaves may be distorted or blistered. Fruit may be mottled.

treatments.ratio: N/A — remove and destroy infected plants immediately

prevention: There is NO CURE for this virus — if a plant is infected, remove and burn it immediately to protect other plants
Use only certified virus-free seeds from a trusted source — the virus can live on seeds for years
Wash your hands thoroughly with soap before touching your plants — this virus easily spreads by touch
Clean and disinfect all your tools (knives, scissors, pruning shears) with 10% bleach solution between plants
Control aphids and other sap-sucking insects which can spread the virus from plant to plant
Do not use tobacco products (bidi, cigarette) near your crops — tobacco mosaic virus is closely related and can infect your plants

Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Vigorous plant with deep green leaves and no signs of stress.
prevention: Continue your regular watering schedule — consistent moisture helps prevent many diseases
Support your plants with stakes or cages to keep fruit and leaves off the ground
Check your plants every week for early signs of blight, leaf spots, or insect damage
Feed with balanced fertilizer at the right growth stage
Keep the area around your plants clean and weed-free

Tomato_leaf.cause: No specific disease detected. The leaf appears normal.
prevention: Continue your regular care routine — proper watering, fertilizing, and pest monitoring
Check leaves weekly for any changes in colour, spots, or unusual patterns
Keep good airflow around your plants by proper spacing and pruning

Tomato_leaf_bacterial_spot.cause: Caused by Xanthomonas species. Spreads rapidly during warm, rainy weather via rain splash and contaminated tools.
Tomato_leaf_bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown with yellow halos. Leaves may drop off.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds from trusted sources
Water at the base of plants only — never from above
Rotate your crops every season
Remove and burn infected leaves and plants immediately
Clean your tools with bleach solution between plants

Tomato_leaf_late_blight.cause: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. Extremely dangerous — can destroy your entire crop in just a few days in cool, wet conditions.
Tomato_leaf_late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked dark patches on leaves that turn black rapidly. White mold visible on leaf underside. Entire plant can collapse.
prevention: URGENT: Act immediately — this disease kills crops within days
Remove and burn all infected plants — do NOT compost them
Spray protective fungicide on healthy plants nearby
Avoid wetting leaves — use drip or base watering only
Plant resistant varieties in the next season

Tomato_leaf_mosaic_virus.cause: Caused by Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV). Spread by touch — through hands, tools, and insects. No chemical cure exists.
Tomato_leaf_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves. Leaves may be distorted. Fruit quality is poor.
prevention: No cure exists — remove and burn infected plants immediately
Wash hands with soap before touching plants
Disinfect all tools with bleach between plants
Use certified virus-free seeds
Do not use tobacco products near your crops

Tomato_leaf_yellow_virus.cause: A viral disease spread by whiteflies. There is no cure — prevention and whitefly control are the only options.
Tomato_leaf_yellow_virus.symptoms: Leaves curl upward and turn yellow. Plants become stunted and produce very little fruit.
prevention: No cure exists — remove and burn infected plants immediately
Control whiteflies aggressively with insecticide sprays and yellow sticky traps
Use insect-proof nets over your seedling nursery
Plant resistant varieties
Do not plant near already-infected fields

Tomato_mold_leaf.cause: Caused by fungus that thrives in high humidity (above 85%) with poor air circulation, commonly seen in greenhouse conditions.
Tomato_mold_leaf.symptoms: Pale yellow patches on upper leaf surface with olive-green to brown velvety mold underneath.
prevention: Reduce humidity by improving ventilation — open doors and windows in greenhouses
Remove infected leaves immediately
Water only at the base of plants
Space plants properly for good air circulation
Use fans in enclosed growing areas to keep air moving

Tomato_two_spotted_spider_mites_leaf.cause: Caused by Two-spotted spider mites. These tiny pests thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
Tomato_two_spotted_spider_mites_leaf.symptoms: Tiny yellow speckles on leaves, fine webbing on leaf underside. Leaves turn bronze and drop off.

treatments.ratio: 5ml liquid soap per litre of water

prevention: Check leaf undersides regularly for tiny mites and webbing
Keep plants well-watered — stressed plants attract mites
Spray water on leaf undersides to wash off mites
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial predator insects
Keep your field clean and dust-free

grape_leaf.cause: No specific disease detected. The leaf appears normal.
prevention: Continue regular care — proper pruning, watering, and pest monitoring
Check leaves regularly for any spots or discolouration
Maintain good airflow through the canopy by proper training and pruning

grape_leaf_black_rot.cause: Caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. Spreads in warm, rainy weather through spores released during rainfall.
grape_leaf_black_rot.symptoms: Reddish-brown circular spots on leaves. Fruit shrivels into hard, black mummies.
prevention: Remove and destroy all shrivelled mummified fruit
Prune for good canopy airflow and sunlight
Start protective fungicide sprays early in the season
Remove all infected leaves from the ground
Keep vines properly trained and not too dense
